title: Exercise Dosing to Retain Resistance Training Adaptations in Young and Older Adults
authors: Bickel CS, Cross JM, Bamman MM
population: 70 adults, young (20-35 years) and older (60-75 years); resistance training 3 days a week for 16 weeks, then 32 weeks of detraining or one of two maintenance doses. Not athletes, not runners.
findings: Phase 1 was resistance training 3 days a week for 16 weeks; phase 2 lasted 32 weeks with random assignment to detraining or to a maintenance dose reduced to one third or one ninth of the phase 1 dose.
Both maintenance doses preserved the phase 1 muscle hypertrophy in the young but not in the older adults; in the young the one-third dose led to additional myofiber hypertrophy.
Strength gained in phase 1 was largely retained throughout detraining, with only a slight reduction at the final time point.
The authors conclude that older adults need a higher weekly dose than the young to keep the myofiber hypertrophy gained, while their gains in specific strength were well preserved.
limitations: Untrained adults who trained for 16 weeks, not athletes in a racing season; the outcomes are muscle mass, fibre size and strength, with no running outcome; the abstract does not give the sizes of the groups or the strength figures. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: Evidence for the direction of a maintenance rule: a cut to a third or a ninth of the training dose kept the muscle gained in young adults, and strength held through 32 weeks of detraining in both ages. It supports a low maintenance dose and a conservative return, not a particular number of sets or sessions.
Older adults needed more than younger ones to keep muscle size, a reason not to cut the maintenance dose by age and to leave the age-related ramp-in as a default.
